item.title: Nepal: “Mud is everywhere”. A Caritas aid worker speaks about the flood that buried a Himalayan valley
item.dc:creator: Susan Dabbous
item.description:

The post Nepal: “Mud is everywhere”. A Caritas aid worker speaks about the flood that buried a Himalayan valley appeared first on Caritas.
item.content:encoded:
Days after catastrophic floods buried whole villages, Caritas Nepal is expanding its humanitarian aid reach. On 26 August, a glacial lake in the Himalayas breached its natural banks in what is known as a glacial lake outburst flood, a sudden release of water, ice and rock triggered when a lake dammed by glacial debris gives way, sending a wall of water and mud crashing down the valleys below.

Days later, Arpana Karki, Programme Coordinator for Caritas Nepal’s Disaster Management Department, explains the response so far, the current needs on the ground, and how communities are coping with the mud left behind. “Mud is everywhere,” she says — and she recounts how one Caritas team became stuck for eighteen hours on their way to deliver aid to Nuwakot.

Did people expect a disaster like this?

Yes, the risk was known as there we knew that more than 2,000 glacial lakes in Nepal, and 21 have been identified as potentially at risk of an outburst. We used to think of it as a distant risk, something that could happen in the future. Now we have already faced it, and the impact is very alarming. The question is no longer whether it will happen, but when the next outburst will come, and whether we are prepared.

How are people describing what happened, in their own words?

People have struggled to find words big enough to describe what they experienced. Some said it was like a tsunami, others like a volcanic storm. Their descriptions may differ, but together they convey just how overwhelming the event was.

How did Caritas respond in the first days?

From the first day, we started coordinating with local partners. On day two our staff started moving with food and non-food items, and we went to see the holding centres and displacement centres. There were a lot of people there, but eventually people started moving on to Kathmandu. Kathmandu is about 70 to 80 kilometres from Nuwakot, so people have been coming there too, and we’ve been addressing their needs as well while trying not to overburden the host communities or encourage negative coping mechanisms.

How many people are still cut off from aid?

It could be more than 2,000 households. People in the urban and semi-urban areas have access to roads and have received aid, but many villages don’t have road access at all. The only possibility for them is helicopters, and we’re trying. We want to reach around 350 households who are still up in the hills with food and non-food items — until yesterday they were saying they only had food for one or two days left.

How are people dealing with the mud?

Mud is everywhere now, from three feet to sixteen or twenty feet deep, inside and outside buildings. Debris clearance has to be one of the first activities for early recovery. I had a meeting yesterday (1 September) with the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, and they agreed we should focus on clearing mud from schools, health facilities and homes so people can live in them again. It’s also making delivery harder — you can see the trucks getting stuck in the mud, and it’s the rainy season, so it’s raining very heavily too.

What happened to the Caritas convoy that got stuck for 18 hours?

One of our young teams, in several trucks, set off from our office in Kathmandu bound for Nuwakot, But the journey took far longer than expected, and they did not reach their destination until well after dark the following day. In total it took them about eighteen hours, carrying mostly dry food — rice, lentils — and non-food items. Around four or five in the evening, they told me that the roads were in terrible condition. It was raining heavily, the roads were narrow, and we were concerned about the risk of soil erosion, so we didn’t want them to continue. They had to stay there overnight, without proper food to eat, and set off again the following morning.

When they finally arrived, people welcomed them with a very big heart. Whenever I called them, they kept saying: “Don’t worry, don’t worry.” They were so positive, even though they hadn’t eaten properly either. They said: “Okay, finally we’ll be able to deliver the stuff” — and their first question was when I was sending them on the next trip. They were already excited to go again.

What trauma is Caritas witnessing on the ground, particularly among women and children?

Just before this call I was speaking to my team in Uttargaya, Rasuwa, Ward Number Five. They told me there are 56 orphaned children there, all cramped into one room, and we were discussing how to support them — with food, non-food items, and even paying rent so they can have two rooms and a teacher or guardian to look after them, because someone has to cook for them too. I don’t think the government will be able to set up an orphanage that quickly.

We don’t yet know how many more orphans there will be across the other villages. The trauma is still very recent, especially for the women, many of whom have lost their husbands, their children, their belongings.

They can’t fully process it yet — right now their priority is getting somewhere safe. It will take time before they can properly grieve. With children, we’ve seen videos where they’re asked where their parents are, and they say they were washed away by the river; asked who they’re staying with, they say a friend or a sister. I think they know something has happened, but they haven’t really understood it yet. Perhaps they are still trying to make sense of what has happened and what it means to be without their parents. That understanding may come later, when the immediate shock has passed and reality begins to sink in.

What is Caritas specifically doing for children?

We’re planning various activities such as nutritious food support, dignity kits, temporary learning shelters, because a lot of schools have been damaged and proper reconstruction will take time. We’ve planned around 20 of these shelters, with psychosocial counselors and teachers, and support them with a kit full of board games and toys so children can play, have fun and have some normality with friends and teachers while they process what’s happened.

If you had one message for international decision-makers on climate change, what would it be?

My message would be simple: don’t just come when disaster happens. Places like Rasuwa need support to rebuild, to prepare for the next disaster, and to make sure people have early-warning systems that can actually save lives. These communities need to be part of long-term development, not forgotten once the headlines fade and the emergency is over. They deserve the chance to recover, rebuild stronger, and be better prepared for what lies ahead. No one should be left behind.

What does Nepal need to face the future with less fear of natural disasters?

It’s always better to help communities prepare in advance than to wait until a disaster has already happened and then try to respond. An early warning is only useful if people receive it in time, understand what it means, and know what action to take. The government also has an important role in planning and zoning. We know there are glacial lakes that could pose a risk, and there are areas where people should not be building homes. We need clear risk zones and better planning so that communities are not put in harm’s way.

Early warning and preparedness should be a major government priority. Organisations like ours can support that by helping communities prepare, practice, and take anticipatory action before a disaster strikes. Ultimately, the goal is not just to respond better, but to make sure fewer people are caught unprepared in the first place.

What Pope Leo’s solidarity message meant to you and your community?

We were very moved to hear Pope Leo’s words and prayers for Nepal, and the contribution that came with them was very symbolic for us, we don’t often receive support like that, so it meant a lot. We are very grateful—not only to Pope Leo, but also to Caritas Internationalis, whose team has been incredibly supportive throughout this difficult time. That solidarity has reminded people here that they are not alone.

By Susan Dabbous, Caritas Internationalis Editorial and Media Officer

item.title: Nepal: Caritas calls for solidarity as climate injustice leaves communities facing devastating floods
item.dc:creator: Susan Dabbous
item.description:

The post Nepal: Caritas calls for solidarity as climate injustice leaves communities facing devastating floods appeared first on Caritas.
item.content:encoded:
A week after the flash floods in Rasuwa district, Caritas Nepal is continuing to reach affected communities with food, essential supplies and other emergency assistance, as heavy rain and damaged roads make access to some areas extremely difficult.  

According to the latest figures, 1,127 people have died and 4,858 remain missing. 

In one case, a Caritas team took 18 hours to reach its destination in Nuwakot, with roads turned into mud and damaged infrastructure making the journey extraordinarily difficult.  

Despite the difficulties, the organisation has provided ready-to-eat meals through more than 50 community kitchens, emergency shelter and essential household items to 1,000 families, as well as water, sanitation and hygiene kits and solar lighting and charging facilities. Caritas is preparing to scale up its assistance to reach up to 4,000 families.

“We are deeply saddened and heartbroken by the severe devastation unfolding in our communities. Our teams are reaching affected communities to deliver immediate food and supplies. Local community kitchens are feeding displaced families, working hand in hand with our local emergency partners, networks and disaster management committees,” – Sister Cecilia Durga Shrestha, Executive Director of Caritas Nepal. 

According to Arpana Karki, Programme Coordinator for Caritas Nepal’s Disaster Management Department, “there are communities who have fled to higher ground and are now staying with host families. Reaching them is extremely difficult, while food supplies are running out.” The only way to reach these communities is by helicopter, which are scarce and in high demand.  

The humanitarian response is also reaching people forced to leave their communities and move towards the capital Katmandu, Caritas is supporting displaced families as they arrive in safer areas, while preparing longer-term assistance including cash-for-work, rent assistance, debris clearance, temporary learning spaces for children and livelihood recovery. 

Caritas Nepal staff have identified 56 orphaned children living in overcrowded shelters and have offered assistance to the government to provide them with safe, appropriate spaces for learning as their communities begin the long process of rebuilding. 

Wake-up call for Climate justice  

 The disaster also exposes a profound climate injustice. “Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet its Himalayan communities are facing increasingly dangerous climate-related risks,” stressed Sister Cecilia in her message for the World Day of Prayer for Creation.

The flash flood was created by the sudden release of water, ice and debris when the glacial dam collapsed and the lake dropped into the Bhote Koshi river system, and scientists warn that rising temperatures are increasing instability across the Himalayas. 

For Caritas Internationalis, Nepal is a stark reminder that those who have contributed least to global emissions are often among those facing the greatest consequences. 

“It is with great sadness that I am following the news of the death and destruction caused by the glacial dam collapse and associated torrent. Our thoughts and prayers are with all those who have died or are suffering as a result.” Alistair Dutton, Secretary General of Caritas Internationalis

According to Dutton: “Europe has been on its knees in the heat all summer and now Nepal is reeling from the devastation of the flash flood released by ice melt that swept through it, taking thousands of lives and homes as it went. We must all face the climate chaos that is so evident all around us and commit to do what is necessary to care for our common home.” He also added:

“The consequences of not dealing with it will be dreadful for all of us, particularly those like the people of Nepal, who have done so little to create this climate emergency. We, the richest, who have prospered from carbon-based energy systems historically, must step up and accept our responsibility for the chaos and harm that we are now seeing in every corner of the globe.”

Urgent needs and global solidarity 

Humanitarian organisations have identified the immediate priorities as safe water, food, healthcare, protection and longer-term shelter.  

With heavy rain hampering relief efforts and winter approaching in the Himalayas, the Caritas network is mobilising support for Caritas Nepal and the communities it serves. 

But beyond the emergency, communities will need sustained support to rebuild safely, restore livelihoods and prepare for a future in which extreme climate-related events are becoming more frequent and difficult to predict.

item.content:encoded:
Job Description

Job position: Caritas Identity and Mission Senior Officer

Job title and functional level: Senior Officer – Level 9

Department: Confederation Development

Line Manager: Director of Confederation Development

Work Place: CI General Secretariat – Palazzo San Callisto

Main Responsibilities

  1. To coordinate, animate and mobilise the Confederation’s Regions and Members, on activities and initiatives which promote Caritas’ identity, vision and mission within and outside the network, in collaboration with the Confederation’s relevant structures (e.g. Caritas Identity and Fraternal Cooperation Committee);
  2. To facilitate and enhance global, regional and national initiatives related to Caritas’ identity, mission and partnership/fraternal cooperation, in cooperation with the Regional Secretariats;
  3. To facilitate and support the implementation of the CI Strategic Framework focusing on the elements related to Caritas identity and mission, through the work of the CI related working structures, and particularly through the work of the Caritas Identity Committee. Implement this work mainly by animating members, contributing to and preparing the necessary related documentation, and supporting discussions and resolutions;
  4. To contribute to the reflection on Caritas’ identity and facilitate the development of induction and training modules on Caritas’ mission and values for leadership, staff, volunteers etc.;
  5. To facilitate activities and initiatives to enhance partnership and fraternal cooperation, and the development of training modules to strengthen and enhance partnership principles across the Caritas network and beyond, in cooperation with the relevant Confederation structures;
  6. To work in collaboration with the relevant Strategic Orientation Committees with regard to topics related to Catholic Social Teaching, Caritas mission, values and principles, and consult with the relevant Confederation’s stakholders on those topics, as needed;
  7. To support relevant stakholders and Confederation’s structures in building and strengthening relationships between Member Organisations and with Bishops’ Conferences, and with other Catholic and faith-based actors;
  8. To work in collaboration with the relevant Holy See Dicasteries, Bishops’ Conferences, other relevant organisations, universities and institutes of higher education to build relationships, enhance promotion and understanding of Caritas identity, vision and mission;
  9. To support the work of strengthening Caritas in the parishes and other faith-based community structures at the grassroots structures;
  10. To contribute to the work on increasing effectiveness of the Caritas Confederation, and collaborate with relevant staff at the CI General Secretariat and relevant bodies at global and regional levels, with specific focus on partnership, values-based leadership and compliance with standards related to identity and mission;
  11. To organise and participate in meetings/events on related topics;
  12. To coordinate and facilitate the work of the CI General Secretariat on Caritas identity, vision and mission, Catholic foundations, consistency with values and principles in the documents produced;
  13. To represent the CI General Secretariat with relevant communities of practice and external stakeholders;
  14. To make sure that activities and initiatives related to the work areas above are in line with the operational plan and budget;
  15. To contribute to the overall work of the Confederation Development Department and to the growth of the team.

PROFILE

  • University degree(s) in a subject related to humanitarian, development, international relations, social sciences, faith-based contexts, and/or other relevant field(s);
  • At least 7 years of professional experience in a Catholic-inspired organisation, including an active role in facilitation, animation, and/or programme management;
  • Deep knowledge and extensive experience of the Church and Caritas structures;
  • Profound experience in the charitable work, also within parish or similar structures;
  • Working proficiency in written and oral English; knowledge of French, Spanish and/or Italian is a strong asset;
  • Knowledge of development and humanitarian issues;
  • Knowledge of organisational development and capacity strengthening processes, developing training modules and facilitating training sessions;
  • Strong analytical, monitoring, evaluation and reporting skills;
  • Capacity to work in a diverse team and a multicultural environment with a spirit of respect and service;
  • Understanding of an “accompanying attitude” and ability to promote it with Regions and Member Organisations;
  • Capacity and willingness to be flexible and to work well under pressure;
  • Capacity and willingness to work with discretion regarding matters of high confidentiality or importance;
  • Ability to communicate clearly and to a high standard (oral and written);
  • Ability to meet assigned deadlines and be results-oriented;
  • Adaptability, flexibility and availability to travel in different countries, even with short-term notice;
  • Proficient computer skills and experience working with Microsoft Office software (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, etc.);
  • Demonstrable empathy and respect for the faith and values of the Catholic Church;
  • Understanding of, and commitment to, the principles of Catholic Social Teaching.


This list of duties and responsibilities is by no means exhaustive, and the post holder may be required to undertake other relevant and appropriate duties as required. This job description is subject to regular review and appropriate modification.

Come and join us and help make a real difference in the lives of the world’s poorest communities.

Caritas Internationalis is committed to safeguarding people from exploitation and abuse in its work and has specific policies on this commitment which outline the expected behaviour and the responsibility of all staff. We follow safe recruitment practices according to our Safeguarding Policies.

Any candidate offered a job at Caritas Internationalis is expected to sign a Code of Conduct and the Safeguarding Policy as an appendix to their contract and agree to conduct themselves in accordance with its provisions.

Please send the CV, the cover letter (English language) and the Job Application by 4th September 2026 (12:00 Rome time) to the attention of Dr. Yari Bergamasco, Human Resources & Legal Affairs Manager, to hr@caritas.va.

Please, note that the interviews for this position will be held by 10 October 2026.
Details will be communicated to shortlisted candidates later.

Important information for non-EU candidates:
Employment is subject to obtaining the necessary entry visa and all required authorizations from the competent authorities, including authorization for health insurance coverage. Please note that this process may take a considerable amount of time and could result in a delayed start date. Should the required visa and/or authorizations not be granted, Caritas Internationalis will be unable to proceed with the appointment.

Download the brochure here

item.content:encoded:
Job Description

Job position: Youth Mobilisation, Empowerment and Inclusion Officer

Job title and functional level: Programme Officer – Level 8

Type of contract: 2-year fixed term contract or secondment from a Caritas Member Organisation

Department: Confederation Development

Line Manager: Inclusive Leadership Senior Officer / Director of the Confederation Development

Work Place: CI General Secretariat – Palazzo San Callisto

Main Responsibilities

  1. To contribute to increasing the effectiveness of the Caritas Confederation by coordinating the work on enhancing youth (aged 18-35) inclusion, empowerment and leadership;
  2. To contribute to develop, and to revise; to implement, monitor and evaluate a Confederation-wide strategy to promote youth empowerment, inclusion and leadership at all levels, as part of the implementation of the CI Strategic Framework. This work is carried out in close coordination with the Inclusive Leadership Senior Officer, who is responsible for developing and overseeing Caritas Internationalis’ long-term strategy on youth inclusion, leadership, and empowerment, and for ensuring continuity of the workstream across Youth Officer contract cycles;
  3. To facilitate and coordinate cross-cutting, inter-department initiatives on youth inclusion and empowerment, and provide support to relevant bodies to ensure that the voices and experiences of young people are known and adequately considered in the Confederation’s work: This includes sensitizing and animating Caritas youth on the most pressing and urgent issues that the Confederation addresses;
  4. To strengthen young people’s capacities to participate in the mission of Caritas at all levels through professional development and spiritual formation initiatives;
  5. To animate and support the Confederation to effectively empower and include young people in their work, leadership, and decision-making at all levels, in coordination with relevant global, regional and national structures;
  6. To facilitate the creation of and support existing regional youth networks, in coordination with the Regional Secretariats, and work with them to identify priorities and best practices;
  7. To animate and mobilize the global Caritas youth network of professionals and volunteers;
  8. To liaise with and provide support to the youth representatives in the various CI governing and strategic bodies, in coordination with the Inclusive Leadership Senior Officer;
  9. To support and facilitate the work of the Confederation’s working structures related to youth (e.g. task forces, working groups, etc.);
  10. To gather, analyse, and share data on youth participation and engagement across the Confederation, and track progress, by identifying strengths, best practices and gaps. Share this data in reports, and circulate this information widely across the Confederation;
  11. To contribute to the work with relevant Holy See Dicasteries, other organisations, universities and institutes of higher education to promote young people and their experiences and perspectives in relevant structures and decision-making process;
  12. To work with the relevant Regional Secretariats and Member Organisations to coordinate and lead Caritas’ youth delegations to global events and initiatives (e.g. World Youth Day festivals);
  13. To communicate Caritas’ youth strategies and actions via Caritas Youth’s social media channels, collaborate with the Department of Engagement to share youth-related initiatives through Caritas’ mainstream communications channels, and provide information on CI’s youth strategy in any relevant forum (e.g. ad limina visits to the office, in meetings with relevant bodies, etc.);
  14. To attend, contribute to, and organise meetings on youth participation/leadership and related subjects both within and outside of the Caritas Confederation;
  15. To contribute to training, workshops and CIMS assessment processes in the area of youth inclusion and empowerment;
  16. To make sure that activities and initiatives related to the work areas above are in line with the operational plan and budget;
  17. To contribute to the overall work of the Confederation Development Department and to the growth of the team.

PROFILE

  • University degree(s) in a subject related to humanitarian aid, development, international relations, social sciences, faith-based contexts, and/or other relevant field(s);
  • At least 5 years of professional and/or volunteering experience in a Caritas/Church organisation, including an active role in animation, and/or programme implementation;
  • Working proficiency in written and oral English; knowledge of French, Spanish and/or Italian is a strong asset;
  • Knowledge of the Church and Caritas structures;
  • Interest in and knowledge of organisational development and capacity strengthening processes, developing training modules and facilitating training sessions;
  • Ability to lead and animate a global programme and develop a sense of ownership of it by all members by synthesizing diverse inputs into a clear, coherent action plan
  • Familiarity with and ability to effectively and creatively use digital platforms that allow for global collaboration (e.g. zoom, shared online documents, social media, etc.);
  • Good understanding of and ability to adapt to current and changing communications trends, especially those used by young people;
  • Strong understanding of global trends and systems that impact and inform Caritas Internationalis’ mission;
  • Strong public communications and speaking skills;
  • Strong analytical, monitoring, evaluation and reporting skills;
  • Capacity to work in a diverse team and a multicultural environment with a spirit of respect and service;
  • Understanding of an “accompanying attitude” and ability to promote it with Member Organisations;
  • Capacity and willingness to be flexible and to work well under pressure;
  • Capacity and willingness to work with discretion regarding matters of high confidentiality or importance;
  • Ability to communicate clearly and to a high standard (oral and written);
  • Ability to meet assigned deadlines and to be results-oriented;
  • Adaptability, flexibility and availability to travel in different countries, even with short-term notice;
  • Proficient computer skills and experience working with Microsoft Office software (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, etc.), and other digital communications platforms (e.g. Zoom, shared online documents, social media, etc.);
  • Demonstrable empathy and respect for the faith and values of the Catholic Church;
  • Understanding of, and commitment to, the principles of Catholic Social Teaching.

Eligibility

This position is part of a youth-focused initiative under the Caritas Internationalis Strategic Framework 2024–2030 and Youth Strategy, aimed at promoting meaningful youth participation and leadership across the Confederation. Applications are invited from candidates aged 18–32 at the time of application. This age requirement ensures that the successful candidate remains within the Caritas Internationalis definition of Youth (18–35 years of age) throughout the expected two-year duration of the assignment and reflects the specific objectives of the initiative and the nature of the role.

Please send the CV, the cover letter (English language) and the Job Application by 4th September 2026 (12:00 Rome time) to the attention of Dr. Yari Bergamasco, Human Resources & Legal Affairs Manager, to hr@caritas.va.

Please, note that the interviews for this position will be held by 10 October 2026.
Details will be communicated to shortlisted candidates later.

Important information for non-EU candidates:
Employment is subject to obtaining the necessary entry visa and all required authorizations from the competent authorities, including authorization for health insurance coverage. Please note that this process may take a considerable amount of time and could result in a delayed start date. Should the required visa and/or authorizations not be granted, Caritas Internationalis will be unable to proceed with the appointment.

item.content:encoded:
Terms of Reference

Consultancy for the Development of Caritas Internationalis Security Policy and Protocols

1. Introduction

Caritas Internationalis (CI) is a global confederation of 162 national member organisations mandated to serve the poor, accompany communities, and respond to humanitarian crises worldwide. The CI General Secretariat, based in Rome, provides Global strategic coordination, representation, policy leadership, and surge support to the confederation.

Secretariat staff regularly travel to member countries, including high‑risk environments affected by conflict, political instability, natural disasters, and other hazards. While many CI members have their own security policies, the Secretariat lacks a dedicated Security Policy and specific protocols governing Secretariat staff, Secretariat operations, Secretariat travel, and Secretariat duty of care that would meet the CI Management Standards.

This consultancy will therefore develop a Caritas Internationalis Secretariat Security Policy and Protocols, ensuring:

  • Clear governance and accountability within the Secretariat
  • Duty‑of‑care standards for Secretariat staff and consultants
  • Alignment with member policies when Secretariat staff travel
  • Coherent crisis coordination mechanisms
  • Integration with safeguarding, HR, and CI governance policies

The policy will not impose requirements on member organisations, but it must define how Secretariat staff operate safely within member contexts and in coordination with member security frameworks.

2. Purpose of the Consultancy

The purpose of this consultancy is to develop a comprehensive, practical, and implementable Security Policy for the CI General Secretariat, accompanied by operational protocols, tools, and guidance.

The policy must:

  • Govern Secretariat staff, Secretariat operations, and Secretariat travel
  • Define how Secretariat staff interface with member security systems
  • Ensure Secretariat duty of care
  • Strengthen Secretariat crisis coordination and preparedness

3. Objectives

3.1 Primary Objectives

  • CI Secretariat Security Policy: Develop a policy defining governance, roles, responsibilities, minimum standards, and duty‑of‑care expectations for Secretariat staff.
  • Operational Protocols & Tools: Produce Secretariat‑specific tools including risk assessment templates, incident reporting pathways, crisis management procedures, and travel security guidelines.
  • Alignment with Standards: Ensure alignment with Catholic Social Teaching, CI governance, safeguarding frameworks, and international humanitarian security standards.
  • Interface with Member Policies: Define how Secretariat staff coordinate with member organisations’ security policies during travel or surge support missions.
  • All secretariat staff training: Based on the policy and protocols, provide all staff of the secretariat with a training on the policy and relevant protocols.

3.2 Secondary Objectives

  • Secretariat Gap Analysis: Assess Secretariat security practices and Secretariat travel procedures.
  • Member Policy Review: Review a sample of member security policies to understand implications for Secretariat travel.
  • Consultations: Facilitate consultations with Secretariat leadership, Regional Secretariats, and selected members.
  • Capacity‑Building Recommendations: Provide recommendations for Secretariat capacity‑building and phased implementation.

3.3 Specific Aspects to Be Covered in the CI Secretariat Security Policy

  • Secretariat Governance & Accountability: Secretariat‑level oversight, reporting lines, decision‑making authority, and escalation pathways.
  • Secretariat Duty of Care:  Obligations toward Secretariat staff, consultants, interns, and volunteers.
  • Secretariat Risk Management Framework: Secretariat‑specific risk assessment, mitigation, and monitoring processes.
  • Travel & Movement Security: Travel approval, pre‑deployment briefings, coordination with member security focal points, compliance with member protocols, movement tracking.
  • Interface with Member Policies: Secretariat staff must follow member security rules when visiting; Secretariat retains duty of care; clarify roles and authority during joint missions.
  • Incident Reporting & Escalation:  Secretariat‑specific incident categories, reporting timelines, and escalation triggers.
  • Secretariat Crisis Management: Secretariat crisis cell, coordination with member crisis structures, surge support protocols, evacuation decision‑making.
  • Evacuation & Relocation: Secretariat‑specific procedures, including coordination with member organisations and external actors.
  • Information Security & Digital Risk: Digital security, data protection, safe communication protocols.
  • Safeguarding Integration: Alignment with CI safeguarding policies, especially during Secretariat travel.
  • HR & Personnel Security: Recruitment screening, mandatory training, psychological support, post‑incident care.
  • Facility & Asset Security: Standards for the CI Secretariat office in Rome.
  • Operational Continuity:  Continuity planning during crises affecting Rome or Secretariat travel.
  • Compliance & Monitoring: Monitoring adherence and improving practices.

4. Scope of Work

4.1 Inception Phase

  • Review Secretariat governance documents, safeguarding policies, HR procedures, and travel protocols.
  • Conduct interviews with Secretariat leadership and selected Regional Secretariats.
  • Deliver an Inception Report outlining methodology and workplan.

4.2 Assessment & Benchmarking

  • Assess Secretariat security practices and Secretariat travel procedures.
  • Review a sample of member security policies to understand implications for Secretariat travel.
  • Benchmark against sector standards (INSO, CHS, ISO 31000, InterAction guidelines).

4.3 Policy Development

Draft the CI Secretariat Security Policy, including:

  • Secretariat governance and accountability
  • Secretariat duty of care
  • Secretariat risk management
  • Secretariat travel and movement security
  • Interface with member security policies
  • Secretariat crisis management
  • Secretariat information security
  • Secretariat HR and personnel security
  • Secretariat facility security
  • Secretariat operational continuity

4.4 Protocols & Tools

Develop Secretariat‑specific tools:

  • Risk Assessment Template
  • Travel Approval & Briefing Forms
  • Incident Reporting Pathways
  • Crisis Management SOPs
  • Evacuation Guidelines
  • Partner‑Coordination Checklist
  • Secretariat Security Plan Template

4.5 Consultation & Validation

  • Facilitate up to three consultation workshops (virtual or hybrid).
  • Integrate feedback from Secretariat, Regional Secretariats, and selected members.

4.6 Finalisation & Handover

  • Deliver final versions of the CI Secretariat Security Policy, Protocols, and Implementation Guidance.
  • Present key elements to CI leadership.

5. Deliverables

  • Inception Report
  • Gap Analysis & Benchmarking Report
  • Draft CI Secretariat Security Policy
  • Draft Operational Protocols and Tools
  • Consultation Workshop Materials & Summary Reports
  • Final CI Secretariat Security Policy
  • Final Operational Protocols and Tools
  • Implementation Roadmap
  • Final Presentation to CI Leadership

6. Timeline

Estimated duration: 12–16 weeks, structured as follows:

  • Inception Phase – 2 weeks
  • Assessment & Benchmarking – 3 weeks
  • Policy Drafting – 3 weeks
  • Protocol Development – 3 weeks
  • Consultations – 2 weeks
  • Finalization – 1 weeks

7. Consultant Profile

The consultant or firm must demonstrate:

  • Experience in security risk management within humanitarian or faith‑based organisations.
  • Proven track record developing security policies for INGOs or confederations.
  • Understanding of Catholic Social Teaching and CI’s mission.
  • Experience in high‑risk environments and crisis coordination.
  • Familiarity with safeguarding, duty of care, and humanitarian standards.
  • Strong facilitation and consultation skills.
  • Ability to produce accessible tools for organisations with varying capacities.

8. Management & Reporting

  • Consultant reports to the Humanitarian and Internal Services Directors.
  • Reference Group includes Secretariat and Regional representatives.
  • Final deliverables approved by the CI Strategic Leadership Team (SLT).

9. Ethical Considerations

The consultant must adhere to:

  • Caritas Internationalis Code of Conduct
  • Safeguarding policies
  • Data protection and confidentiality requirements
  • Do‑no‑harm and humanitarian ethics

10. Application Requirements

Applicants must submit:

  • Technical proposal
  • Financial proposal
  • CVs of key personnel
  • Examples of similar work
  • 2 References

item.title: Caritas Indonesia stands with the communities affected by the earthquake
item.dc:creator: Susan Dabbous
item.description:

Since a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off Flores Island, one of the Lesser Sunda Islands […]

The post Caritas Indonesia stands with the communities affected by the earthquake appeared first on Caritas.
item.content:encoded:
As the death toll from the magnitude 7.7 earthquake reaches 100 and more than 160,000 people remain displaced, Caritas Indonesia has been on the ground since the start of the humanitarian emergency, bringing food, shelter and hope to affected communities.

Since a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off Flores Island, one of the Lesser Sunda Islands in Indonesia’s East Nusa Tenggara province, before dawn on 15 August, communities have not stopped moving.

The 15 August earthquake was followed six days later by a further magnitude 5.8 aftershock centred inland.

“People are so afraid,” explains Fr. Fredy Rante Taruk, Executive Director of Caritas Indonesia, “they don’t want to go back to their homes.” More than 160,000 people are currently displaced, with over 57,000 homes damaged. “Most of them live in tents; they don’t dare to stay in their homes because they are scared of the aftershocks.”

“That’s why people really need tents, blankets, clean water, food, water sanitation and, above all, medicines.” – Fr. Fredy Rante Taruk, Executive Director of Caritas Indonesia

The disaster’s impact stretches well beyond Flores itself, with damage recorded across nine areas. According to the latest figures from Indonesia’s National Search and Rescue Agency, aside from the civilian homes, hundreds of schools, health facilities and 195 houses of worship have been damaged, as aftershocks are expected to continue shaking the island for several more weeks.

From the very first hours, Caritas Indonesia activated a National Network-scale response, formally designating the disaster Impact Scale Level III and opening Emergency Response Service Posts across the four affected dioceses. The organisation immediately mobilised its medical teams and opened logistics posts in Surabaya and Kupang to channel aid — including water tanks, tents and construction materials — to Flores.

The Archdiocese of Ende, covering Nagekeo and Ngada Regencies on the island’s southern coast and among the hardest-hit, has focused on damage assessment across parishes battered by intensity VII shaking, with at least 20 buildings damaged, including in Ndona and Aeramo. Service posts, including a dedicated shelter for the elderly, have been set up as residents remain wary of returning indoors.

The diocese of Maumere, based in Sikka Regency on Flores’s north-eastern coast, has coordinated closely with the local Health Office to run a health post at the Samador Field evacuation site, currently supported by a doctor, a pharmacy worker and two nurses — though capacity is stretched thin.

The diocese of Ruteng, seat of Manggarai Regency in the island’s mountainous west, saw more than 50 buildings damaged, including Ruteng Cathedral. Teams moved swiftly to evacuate hospital patients into emergency tents and have been gathering casualty data alongside the parish network.

The diocese of Labuan Bajo, the gateway town at Flores’s western tip near Komodo National Park, has focused on shelter kits and psychosocial support, though patchy connectivity continues to hamper efforts to reach outlying parishes.

Caritas delivered 180 kg of medicines

Caritas Indonesia has also mobilised a national medical team, distributing 180kg of medicines and medical equipment to meet the needs of the survivors and displaced persons at the disaster site, with additional doctors and nurses deployed to reinforce health services in the Archdiocese of Ende and the Diocese of Ruteng.

Children have been among those most affected by the earthquake and its thousands of aftershocks. Caritas volunteers and religious sisters provide psychosocial activities for children, while offering parents Psychological First Aid, group support and spiritual care to help them cope with post-disaster anxiety.

For Fr. Fredy, the response has been effective. “In a situation like this, the Catholic Church acts in unison, coordinating with local government authorities,” he said, describing how bishops, priests, religious sisters and lay volunteers across the four dioceses opened their doors within hours of the quake.

To sustain the humanitarian response, Caritas Surabaya and the Archdiocese of Kupang opened aid collection points in Surabaya and Kupang, where they are gathering donations of food, hygiene kits and other essential supplies from the public before shipping them on to Flores.

“I am grateful that the coordination among the diocesan Caritas is proceeding smoothly this is enabling us to rapidly provide for the needs of the affected residents,” Fr. Fredy Rante Taruk, Executive Director of Caritas Indonesia

As rehabilitation and reconstruction planning begins, Caritas Indonesia continues to call on the wider Caritas family and the international community to stand with the affected communities in the months ahead.

item.title: How Caritas is supporting communities affected by Ebola in the DRC
item.dc:creator: Susan Dabbous
item.description:

The outbreak continues to spread in the east of the country, driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there is currently no licensed vaccine or approved treatment. The World Health Organization […]

The post How Caritas is supporting communities affected by Ebola in the DRC appeared first on Caritas.
item.content:encoded:
Three months after the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared its 17th Ebola outbreak on 15 May 2026, the situation remains deeply concerning. The outbreak continues to spread in the east of the country, driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there is currently no licensed vaccine or approved treatment.

The World Health Organization is currently assessing whether existing Ebola vaccines and available treatments could be effective against this strain.

As of mid-August 2026, authorities have recorded 4,945 confirmed cases and 2,325 deaths — a case fatality rate of 46 per cent — across six provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo and Bas-Uélé. Declared on 15 May, the outbreak passed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days, making it the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record.

Caritas Congo ASBL is working through its diocesan networks, parishes and community health structures to support affected families, promote prevention and strengthen the response.

Drawing on long-standing relationships with local communities, Caritas teams are helping to build trust, share reliable information and ensure that people affected by the outbreak are not left alone. Abbé Edouard Makimba Milambo, Executive Secretary of Caritas Congo ASBL, recently spoke to the news outlet Crux. Below is a summary of the interview.

The United Nations has described this outbreak as the largest and fastest-spreading ever recorded, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus. From Caritas’ perspective in eastern DRC, does that description match the reality on the ground?

Yes, unfortunately, that description matches what Caritas teams are observing alongside the diocesan Caritas structures concerned. Behind the figures are families living in anguish, villages whose habits have been turned upside down, and health workers operating under intense pressure.

The epidemic is progressing rapidly, cases are touching several health zones, and local capacities are already stretched thin. In eastern DRC, population displacement, insecurity, mobility linked to mining activity and the fragility of the health system are making the outbreak considerably harder to control. For Caritas Congo ASBL, this situation represents a health emergency, a social crisis and a major challenge for communities, all at once.

What impact is this epidemic having on people’s daily lives and on the health system?

The impact is profound and is felt in households’ everyday lives. Families live with the fear of the disease, of losing a loved one, or of prolonged isolation. Markets are running at a slower pace, some small traders are seeing their custom shrink, and day labourers can lose their main source of income. In the most vulnerable households, that loss of income quickly translates into food insecurity.

Health centres, already short of staff, equipment and medicines, must strengthen infection prevention and control measures while still delivering essential care.

“One of the most worrying consequences is that some people are delaying seeking care for fear of being identified as suspected cases.”

Can you share an example or a testimony from a member of your team that illustrates what affected families are currently going through?

An example that comes up often in our exchanges with local teams in the affected dioceses is that of families struck by several bereavements within a few days, while also having to cope with isolation, fear from their neighbours, and uncertainty about tomorrow.

“We are told of parents who can no longer hold their children in their arms during treatment or follow-up, of children who do not understand why a relative has been taken away, and of families who must accept dignified and safe burial measures even as they are living through immense grief.”

These measures are not rejected because families refuse to protect the community; they are sometimes difficult to accept because they touch on very sensitive cultural, spiritual and family practices. That is where our pastoral, social and community presence takes on its full meaning: listening, explaining, accompanying, and helping families feel that they are not alone.

How do you convince terrified populations to trust medical interventions?

Caritas’s strength lies in being present alongside communities well before crises hit. Through parishes, diocesan structures, community outreach workers and faith-based health centres, we often share in people’s daily lives.

“In practical terms, we take the time to listen to concerns, to answer questions in local languages, and to work with people the community trusts: priests, religious sisters and brothers, community leaders, women leaders, young people and survivors. When a message is carried by someone the community knows and respects, it is better understood and better accepted.”

Trust is built when families understand that the measures being proposed are meant to protect them, preserve their dignity and save lives.

As traditional donors scale back their support, who is financing the response to the epidemic today? 

At this stage, the response is being coordinated by the DRC government, with support from WHO, the United Nations system, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), and numerous technical, financial, humanitarian and faith-based partners. Within the Caritas Internationalis network, organisations such as Caritas International Belgium, CRS, CAFOD, Trócaire, Caritas Germany, Secours Catholique-Caritas France, Caritas Spain, Caritas Italiana and Caritas Austria are providing valuable financial, technical, institutional and humanitarian support.

Despite this backing, needs remain significant, particularly around community mobilisation, psychosocial support, local logistics, prevention and the long-term strengthening of health structures. At this stage, Caritas is observing above all a growing strain on local structures, which must respond to rising needs with limited means. We cannot say that health centres have closed purely because of budget cuts. What is clear, however, is that some essential activities can be slowed, delayed or placed under heavy pressure when funding is not available in time. That risks weakening the effectiveness of the response and making it harder to protect the most vulnerable populations.

Sustained resource mobilisation remains essential to guarantee an effective response and protect the most vulnerable populations.

What concrete actions is Caritas currently carrying out on the ground in eastern DRC to slow the virus’s spread and support affected communities?

Caritas contributes mainly to community mobilisation, awareness-raising on prevention measures, the dissemination of reliable messages, referring suspected cases to the appropriate services, and supporting affected families. Concretely, that means going out to communities, engaging with local leaders, explaining warning signs, encouraging handwashing, supporting acceptance of contact tracing, accompanying bereaved families, and helping to reduce the stigmatisation of people who are infected or have recovered. Through its parish, diocesan and health networks, Caritas also helps build acceptance of medical interventions by showing that the response is not imposed on communities but built together with them. For Caritas Congo ASBL, hope rests on solidarity, trust and the conviction that every life saved is the result of a collective effort.

The full interview by reporter Ngala Killian Chimtom, published on Crux, 7 August 2026, is available at this link.

item.title: Why protecting humanitarian workers means protecting humanitarian law
item.dc:creator: Susan Dabbous
item.description:
Every year on 19 August, the international community marks World Humanitarian Day to honour humanitarian workers supporting communities affected by crises and conflicts. At a time of record levels of violence against them, Caritas Internationalis highlights the role of religious actors in promoting respect for international humanitarian law. On this World Humanitarian Day, we pay […]

The post Why protecting humanitarian workers means protecting humanitarian law appeared first on Caritas.
item.content:encoded:
Every year on 19 August, the international community marks World Humanitarian Day to honour humanitarian workers supporting communities affected by crises and conflicts. At a time of record levels of violence against them, Caritas Internationalis highlights the role of religious actors in promoting respect for international humanitarian law.

On this World Humanitarian Day, we pay heartfelt tribute to all those who have lost their lives while carrying out humanitarian work.

This day is a reminder that respect for International Humanitarian Law (IHL) is essential to ensuring the protection of those serving in conflict zones. When a humanitarian worker is deliberately targeted, it is not only an attack on an individual, but also on the humanitarian principles and the international legal framework that safeguard human dignity in times of war.

Humanitarian workers under attack

Over the past three years, more than 1,000 humanitarian workers have been killed around the world. Among them are several members of the Caritas family, including Caritas staff who lost their lives in Mariupol and Gaza, among others.

Most recently, on 26 July, Yana Zhernovskaya, a social worker with Caritas Kharkiv, was killed when a Russian missile struck her home. Her 10-year-old son was injured in the same attack. These tragedies highlight the immense dangers faced by humanitarian workers every day.

According to the United Nations, the war in Gaza has reached the highest level of violence against humanitarian personnel ever recorded in modern history. Despite the danger, Caritas continues to serve in Gaza, where humanitarian workers carry out their daily mission with extraordinary commitment and courage despite the constant risk to their lives.

Watch the video:

These events remind us that the existence of legal rules alone is not enough to ensure compliance. Protecting humanitarian workers also depends on fostering respect for the principles of international humanitarian law within societies and strengthening community ownership of those principles.

The moral force of faith-based advocacy

In this regard, faith-based organisations and religious leaders have a vital role to play. Deeply rooted in their communities, they often enjoy trusted relationships and moral authority that enable them to promote the values of international humanitarian law in ways that resonate across different audiences.

Their commitment to peace, the protection of civilians, and respect for every human life and human dignity can help strengthen support for humanitarian principles. As highlighted in the report Strengthening the Moral Force of International Humanitarian Law Through Faith-based Advocacy—produced by the Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies in Geneva in collaboration with Caritas Internationalis, ACT Alliance and the World Council of Churches—combining humanitarian expertise with the credibility of religious leaders makes advocacy for respect for international humanitarian law significantly more effective.

The Central African Republic: faith leaders on the frontline

The Central African Republic offers a powerful example of the role faith leaders can play in promoting peace despite persistent violence. For more than a decade, the country has endured successive humanitarian crises. In the eastern regions, tensions have escalated further since May 2025, creating new threats to civilian populations. At the same time, shrinking humanitarian funding and the gradual withdrawal of some international actors have significantly reduced operational capacity.

Against this backdrop, the Catholic Church continues to stand alongside the country’s most isolated communities. Bishop Aurelio Gazzera of Bangassou, who has served in the Central African Republic for many years, bears witness to this reality and to the risks faced by those who choose to remain with communities in times of conflict.

The recent killing of Fr Crépin Martial Monga, murdered in his diocese because of his commitment to peace, is a tragic illustration of these dangers. Fr Monga was killed in Zémio, in the Haut-Mbomou region of south-eastern Central African Republic, an area devastated by ethnic conflict between rival local militias. Widely respected as a mediator between armed groups and the authorities, his killing— for which no one has claimed responsibility —reflects the growing dangers facing peacebuilders and humanitarian actors alike.

Bishop Aurelio Gazzera: “Dialogue is key”

Despite the very real threats, we continue because we are among the few who have the strength and courage to do so,
Bishop Aurelio Gazzera

He refers to the role of the Catholic Church and other faith communities in a context where opportunities for dialogue remain extremely limited. Communities often have few means of making their voices heard or reporting the abuses they endure. Religious leaders therefore become essential interlocutors, able to amplify these testimonies and keep channels of dialogue open.

This ability to engage with different stakeholders is one of the greatest strengths of the Interreligious Platform for Peace, which brings together senior Catholic, Muslim and Evangelical leaders. According to Bishop Gazzera, the platform has enabled open dialogue with government authorities, armed forces and local communities, contributing to a better understanding of the conflict and tangible improvements on the ground.

Experience shows that calls to respect international humanitarian law are far more likely to be heard when they are grounded in relationships of trust and a deep understanding of local realities. Through the legitimacy they have earned within their communities, their long-standing presence among affected populations and the neutrality often attributed to them, religious leaders can reach conflict actors who remain inaccessible to many humanitarian organisations and help promote peace.

By combining the strengths and expertise of humanitarian and faith actors, the principles of international humanitarian law can truly come to life. Humanitarian organisations bring technical expertise in protection and international humanitarian law, while religious leaders contribute their deep knowledge of local contexts, their proximity to communities and the trust they have built over many years.

Together, this complementary partnership helps translate humanitarian principles into everyday realities, strengthens respect for international humanitarian law and contributes to better protecting those who risk their lives every day to assist people affected by conflict.

Because behind every protected humanitarian worker are entire communities that can continue receiving the assistance and support they desperately need. Protecting humanitarian workers means protecting life, dignity and hope for people caught up in conflict.

By Anaïs Jeanjean, European and International Studies, Sorbonne Nouvelle University, Paris

item.content:encoded:
JOB DESCRIPTION

Job position: Inclusive Leadership Senior Officer

Job title and functional level: Senior Officer – Level 9

Department: Confederation Development

Line Manager: Director of Confederation Development

Work Place: CI General Secretariat – Palazzo San Callisto

 

MAIN RESPONSIBILITIES

Inclusive leadership

  1. To coordinate and oversee a Confederation-wide strategy on inclusive leadership, based on the following pillars: people (the person at the center, with particular focus on women and youth), policies, enhancing organisational inclusion culture that facilitates participation;
  2. To promote and oversee cross-cutting and inter-department initiatives on inclusiveness and particularly on women’s and youth participation and leadership;
  3. To promote and oversee Confederation’s initiatives at local, regional and global levels to increase leadership opportunities for women and youth from grassroots to governance, in coordination with the Confederation’s relevant structures;
  4. To enhance collaboration with the relevant Holy See Dicasteries, other international organisations, universities and institutes of higher education on initiatives and resources related to inclusiveness, particularly the promotion of women and youth in leadership and decision making;
  5. To develop policies and Confederation’s official documents enhancing inclusive leadership, in line with Caritas’ values, principles and mission, increase visibility of the Confederation’s work in this area, addressing challenges, demonstrating results and celebrating them ;
  6. To support and enhance the Confederation’s work on Leadership Standards (e.g. Leadership Charter dissemination and application within the framework of the position’s mandate, development and facilitation of training modules/sessions for leaders, etc.);
  7. To facilitate dialogue with internal and external key stakholders on the topic;
  8. To contribute to training, workshops and incorporation of the principle of inclusion in assessment tools, and specifically women’s and youth promotion, enhancing peer to peer support and institutional development and capacity strengthening of Caritas Member organisations and Regions.

Women’s Participation, Leadership and Empowerment

  1. To contribute to increasing the effectiveness of the Caritas Confederation by coordinating the overall work on enhancing women’s participation, leadership and empowerment;
  2. To develop/revise and implement the Confederation’s strategy to promote women’s participation and leadership at all levels, as part of the implementation of the CI Strategic Framework;
  3. To support and facilitate the work of the Confederation’s working structures related to women (e.g. task forces, working groups, etc.)
  4. To sensitize Confederation’s stakeholders on women’s participation, leadership and empowerment, by promoting institutional initiatives and increasing visibility of the topic;
  5. To develop and promote workshops, training modules, sensitization and formation initiatives on strengthening ledership skills and enhance leadership pathways;
  6. To promote, support and develop policies and internal mechanism that enhance women’s participation and leadership and learning pathways
  7. To facilitate the development and strengthening of women’s regional focal points/groups, animate the newtwork and work with them in order to identify priority needs and best practices;
  8. To gather, process and analyse data on women’s participation at all levels of the Confederation (national, regional, global) in order to identify strengths and gaps, measure progress, produce relevant documents, research and reports. Report data to the governance level of the Confederation;

To organise and participate in key meetings/events on women’s participation and leadership related issues.

Youth Inclusion, Leadership and Empowerment

  1. To develop, revise and oversee the long-term strategy on youth inclusion, leadership and empowerment, according to the CI Strategic Framework and the indications of the governing bodies;
  2. To promote and oversee the global, long-term strategic work on youth inclusion, leadership and empowerment, by working closely with CI Youth Officer;
  3. To ensure that youth inclusion and empowerment is addressed as a cross-cutting topic and integrated in a transversal way across Confederation’s activities;
  4. To ensure that work on youth is developed based on the key pillars of: policy development; capacity strengthening, targeted training and leadership pathways; mobilisation of the network of youth professional and volunteers;
  5. To support and coordinate with the Youth Officer in liaising with youth representatives in the various CI governing and strategic bodies, fostering effective engagement on strategic and institutional matters;
  6. To lead the biennial onboarding and knowledge transfer process for the incoming Youth Officer, ensuring they are continuously empowered with the tools, knowledge, and support needed to successfully lead the youth workstreams under their responsibility.

Coordination

  1. To make sure that activities and initiatives related to the work areas above are in line with the operational plan and budget;
  2. To oversee the work of the Youth Officer, providing strategic support, ensuring the effective delivery of youth related priorities and integration in the departmental planning and activities, alignment with the CI Strategic Framework, and the continuity of youth engagement and representation throughout role transitions;
  3. To contribute to the overall work of the Confederation Development Department and to the growth of the team.

PROFILE

  • University degree(s) in a subject related to humanitarian, development, international relations, social sciences, faith-based contexts, and/or other relevant field(s);
  • At least 7 years of professional experience, including an active role in strategy development, facilitation, coordination, and/or programme management;
  • Working proficiency in written and oral English; knowledge of French, Spanish and/or Italian is a strong asset;
  • Knowledge and experience in inclusiveness, equality, leadership promotion;
  • Experience in implementation/coordination of women’s and youth programmes is a strong asset;
  • Knowledge of the Church and Caritas structures is an asset;
  • Interest in and knowledge of development and humanitarian issues;
  • Interest in and knowledge of organisational development and capacity strengthening processes, developing training modules and facilitating training sessions;
  • Knowledge of research methods, data analysis and reporting;
  • Strong understanding of global trends and systems that impact and inform Caritas Internationalis’ mission;
  • Ability to coordinate and oversee a global cross-cutting programme and develop a sense of ownership of it by all members;
  • Strong analytical, monitoring, evaluation and reporting skills;
  • Capacity to work in a diverse team and a multicultural environment with a spirit of respect and service;
  • Understanding of an “accompanying attitude” and ability to promote it with Member Organisations;
  • Capacity and willingness to be flexible and to work well under pressure;
  • Capacity and willingness to work with discretion regarding matters of high confidentiality or importance;
  • Ability to communicate clearly and to a high standard (oral and written);
  • Ability to meet assigned deadlines and be results-oriented;
  • Adaptability, flexibility and availability to travel in different countries, even with short-term notice;
  • Demonstrated ability to supervise and support staff, fostering a collaborative and empowering environment that enables individuals to work to the best of their ability.
  • Proficient computer skills and experience working with Microsoft Office software (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, etc.), and other digital communications platforms (e.g. Zoom);
  • Demonstrable empathy and respect for the faith and values of the Catholic Church;
  • Understanding of, and commitment to, the principles of Catholic Social Teaching.

 

This list of duties and responsibilities is by no means exhaustive, and the post holder may be required to undertake other relevant and appropriate duties as required. This job description is subject to regular review and appropriate modification.

Come and join us and help make a real difference in the lives of the world’s poorest communities.

Caritas Internationalis is committed to safeguarding people from exploitation and abuse in its work and has specific policies on this commitment which outline the expected behaviour and the responsibility of all staff. We follow safe recruitment practices according to our Safeguarding Policies.

Any candidate offered a job at Caritas Internationalis is expected to sign a Code of Conduct and the Safeguarding Policy as an appendix to their contract and agree to conduct themselves in accordance with its provisions.

Please send the CV, the cover letter (English language) and the Job Application by 4th September 2026 (12:00 Rome time) to the attention of Dr. Yari Bergamasco, Human Resources & Legal Affairs Manager, to hr@caritas.va.

Please, note that the interviews for this position will be held by 10 October 2026.
Details will be communicated to shortlisted candidates later.

Important information for non-EU candidates:
Employment is subject to obtaining the necessary entry visa and all required authorizations from the competent authorities, including authorization for health insurance coverage. Please note that this process may take a considerable amount of time and could result in a delayed start date. Should the required visa and/or authorizations not be granted, Caritas Internationalis will be unable to proceed with the appointment.

item.dc:creator: Susan Dabbous

The post “The water took everything”: Caritas Pakistan races against the floods appeared first on Caritas.
item.content:encoded:
As monsoon rains hit Pakistan for the twelfth time this season, families are losing homes, crops and livestock. Caritas Pakistan’s director, Amjad Gulzar, describes a humanitarian emergency accelerating faster than the country can respond and an appeal for help before the next downpour arrives.

Pakistan, home to 240 million people, is famed for landscapes that range from the fertile plains of Punjab to the glacier-studded peaks of Gilgit-Baltistan, near K2, the world’s second-highest mountain. But in recent years, flooding has dominated the headlines instead, leaving little room for the beauty and raising the alarm over the humanitarian toll such catastrophic inundations leave behind. Caritas is among the organisations with a plan to prepare for and respond to these increasingly violent climate events, year after year.

 

Since the south-west monsoon broke on 28 June 2026, the country has endured another unusually violent rainy season: what is normally five or six spells of monsoon rain has, this year, stretched to around twelve. Flash floods, landslides and glacial lake outbursts have torn through Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, Balochistan and Azad Jammu & Kashmir. On 3 August, the death toll stood at 145, with hundreds more injured and over a thousand homes destroyed or damaged.

Amjad Gulzar, director of Caritas Pakistan, spoke to us about the human cost and his organisation’s response.

Can you give us an update on the situation on the ground, and how Caritas Pakistan is responding?

It is critical. Rising floodwaters have forced entire villages to evacuate. Some families have reached government relief camps; others are still sleeping in the open, with no protection from further rain. Mud houses have simply collapsed, and even concrete homes have been damaged. In Punjab alone, nearly 400 square kilometres of land — around Sheikhupura, Muridke and Gujranwala — have gone underwater, and more than 94 villages have been affected. In the north, Chitral was hit again in August by flash floods linked to a glacial lake outburst, cutting off communities and killing at least two people.

We’ve activated our full emergency response: Disaster Management Committees, trained volunteers and diocesan teams are on the ground helping people evacuate, protect their belongings and access relief. We’re distributing food, hygiene kits and safe drinking water, and running medical camps for the injuries and waterborne illnesses that follow every flood.

Has the impact of extreme weather in Pakistan been worsening and why?

Undoubtedly. Pakistan is among the countries most exposed to climate change. Rising temperatures are accelerating glacier melt in the north, swelling our rivers, while monsoon rainfall is becoming more erratic and intense. This year’s forecasts pointed to above-normal rain, and events have outpaced even that. It isn’t just about rainfall; it’s about livelihoods. Farmers have lost rice, cotton, sesame and vegetable crops; hundreds of livestock have died, and those that survive face fodder shortages. For families who depend entirely on the land, that is deeply distressing; it’s the end of a lifelong endeavour.

What would you ask of the wider Caritas Confederation and the international community?

We need solidarity and international support to continue our work. Displaced families need shelter kits, food and clean water immediately. But we also need support for early warning systems and community-based preparedness, because these events are no longer occasional: they are becoming the new normal for Pakistan. We are asking our partners to help us respond today, and to help Pakistan build resilience for the floods still to come as we adapt to the new climate.
